englishChanges.before: Mr. Covey's real talent was for deception. His whole life was given over to planning and pulling off the crudest lies. Whatever learning or religion he had, he bent to fit his urge to deceive. He seemed to believe he could even deceive God Almighty. He would say a short prayer in the morning and a long one at night, and, strange as it sounds, few men could at times look more devout than he did. The family worship always opened with singing, and since he was a wretched singer himself, the job of starting the hymn usually fell to me. He would read out the hymn and nod for me to begin. Sometimes I would; other times I would not. My refusal almost always threw everything into confusion. To show he did not need me, he would launch in and lurch through the hymn in the most off-key way imaginable. In that frame of mind he prayed with even more than his usual fervor. Poor man — such was his nature, and his skill at deceiving, that I honestly believe he sometimes fooled himself into the solemn conviction that he was a sincere worshipper of the Most High God; and this at a time when he could be said to be forcing his woman slave into the sin of adultery. Here are the facts. Mr. Covey was a poor man just starting out in life, able to afford only one slave, and — shocking as it is — he bought her, by his own account, as a breeder. The woman's name was Caroline. He bought her from Mr. Thomas Lowe, who lived about six miles from St. Michael's. She was large and strong, around twenty years old, and had already borne one child, which proved her to be exactly what he was after. After buying her, he hired a married man from Mr. Samuel Harrison to live with him for a year, and every night he locked the man up with her. The result was that at the end of the year the poor woman gave birth to twins. This outcome seemed to delight Mr. Covey, both with the man and with the wretched woman. So great was the joy of him and his wife that nothing they could do for Caroline during her confinement was too good or too much trouble. The children were counted as a fine addition to his wealth.

Here are the facts. Mr. Covey was a poor man just starting out in life, able to afford only one slave, and — shocking as it is — he bought her, by his own account, as _a breeder_. The woman's name was Caroline. He bought her from Mr. Thomas Lowe, who lived about six miles from St. Michael's. She was large and strong, around twenty years old, and had already borne one child, which proved her to be exactly what he was after. After buying her, he hired a married man from Mr. Samuel Harrison to live with him for a year, and every night he locked the man up with her. englishChanges.before: Mr. Covey was at the house, about a hundred yards from the treading-yard where we were fanning. The moment he heard the fan stop, he came straight over to where we were and hurriedly demanded to know what was wrong. Bill told him I was sick and there was no one left to bring wheat to the fan. By then I had crawled off under the post-and-rail fence that enclosed the yard, hoping to ease my misery by getting out of the sun. He asked where I was, and one of the hands told him. He came to the spot, looked at me a while, and asked what the matter was. I answered as best I could, for I barely had the strength to speak. At that he kicked me savagely in the side and ordered me to get up. I tried, but fell back. He kicked me again and told me again to rise. I tried once more and managed to get to my feet — but as I bent to grab the tub I had been feeding the fan with, I staggered and went down again. While I lay there, Mr. Covey picked up the hickory slat Hughes had been using to strike off the half-bushel measure and brought it down hard on my head, opening a large gash that bled freely; and with that he again told me to get up. I made no move to obey, having now made up my mind to let him do his worst. A short while after that blow, my head began to clear, and Mr. Covey had by then left me to my own devices. At that moment I decided, for the first time, to go to my master, lodge a complaint, and ask for his protection. To do it I would have to walk seven miles that afternoon, which under the circumstances was a brutal undertaking. I was terribly weak — as much from the kicks and blows as from the fierce attack of sickness I had been through. Still, I watched my chance, and while Covey was looking the other way, I set out for St. Michael's. I had gotten a fair distance on my way toward the woods when Covey spotted me and shouted for me to come back, threatening what he would do if I refused. I ignored both his calls and his threats and pushed on toward the woods as fast as my feeble state allowed; and thinking he might overtake me if I stayed on the road, I went through the woods, keeping far enough from the road to avoid being seen but close enough not to lose my way. I had not gone far before my little strength failed me again. I could go no farther. I fell down and lay there a long while, the blood still seeping from the wound on my head. For a time I thought I would bleed to death, and I believe I would have, had the blood not matted my hair enough to close the wound. After lying there about three-quarters of an hour, I steadied myself again and started on, through bogs and briars, barefoot and bareheaded, tearing my feet at nearly every step; and after a journey of about seven miles that took some five hours to make, I reached my master's store. The state I was in would have moved anyone but a heart of iron. From the top of my head to my feet I was covered in blood — my hair clotted with dust and blood, my shirt stiff with it. I must have looked like a man who had broken out of a den of wild beasts and barely gotten away. Looking like that, I stood before my master and humbly begged him to step in with his authority and protect me. I told him the whole story as well as I could, and as I spoke it seemed at times to move him. He would pace the floor and try to excuse Covey by saying he supposed I must have deserved it. He asked what I wanted. I told him I wanted a new home, because as sure as I lived with Mr. Covey again I would only live with him to die with him; Covey would surely kill me, and was well on the way to it. Master Thomas laughed off the notion that Covey was any danger to my life, said he knew the man, that he was a good man, and that he could not think of taking me away from him — that if he did, he would lose the whole year's wages, that I belonged to Covey for a year and had to go back to him no matter what, and that I had better not bother him with any more such stories, or he would get hold of me himself. After threatening me like that, he gave me a huge dose of salts, told me I could stay in St. Michael's that night, since it was already quite late, but that I had to be off back to Mr. Covey's first thing in the morning — and that if I wasn't, he would get hold of me, which meant he would whip me. I stayed the night, and as ordered I set out for Covey's in the morning, Saturday morning, worn out in body and broken in spirit. I had no supper that night and no breakfast that morning. I reached Covey's around nine o'clock; and just as I was climbing over the fence that separated Mrs. Kemp's fields from ours, out ran Covey with his cowskin to give me another whipping. Before he could get to me, I made it into the cornfield, and since the corn was very high it gave me a place to hide. He looked furious and searched for me a long time. My behavior must have seemed completely senseless to him. Finally he gave up the hunt, figuring, I suppose, that I would have to come home eventually for something to eat, and he would waste no more effort looking. I spent most of that day in the woods, with only two choices before me — go home and be whipped to death, or stay in the woods and starve. That night I ran into Sandy Jenkins, a slave I knew a little. Sandy had a free wife who lived about four miles from Mr. Covey's, and since it was Saturday he was on his way to see her. I told him my situation, and he kindly invited me to go home with him. I went, and we talked the whole matter over while I asked his advice on what I should do. I found Sandy an old hand at giving counsel. He told me very solemnly that I had to go back to Covey, but that before I did, I should go with him to another part of the woods where there was a certain root which, if I carried a piece of it always on my right side, would make it impossible for Mr. Covey, or any other white man, to whip me. He said he had carried it for years, and ever since he had, he had never taken a blow and never expected to as long as he kept it. At first I dismissed the idea that simply carrying a root in my pocket could do any such thing, and I was reluctant to take it; but Sandy pressed the matter earnestly, telling me it could do no harm even if it did no good. To please him I finally took the root and carried it on my right side as he had directed. This was Sunday morning. I started straight for home, and as I came into the yard gate, out came Mr. Covey, on his way to meeting. He spoke to me very kindly, told me to drive the pigs out of a nearby lot, and went on toward church. Now, this strange behavior of Mr. Covey's really did start me wondering whether there was something to the root Sandy had given me; and had it been any day but Sunday, I could have put his manner down to nothing but the power of that root. As it was, I was half ready to believe the root was more than I had first taken it for. All went well until Monday morning, when the root's power was truly put to the test. Long before daylight I was called to go and rub down, curry, and feed the horses. I obeyed, and was glad to. But while I was at it, just as I was tossing down some blades from the loft, Mr. Covey came into the stable with a long rope; and just as I was halfway out of the loft, he grabbed my legs and was about to tie me. As soon as I realized what he was up to, I gave a sudden lunge, and as I did, with him still gripping my legs, I came sprawling onto the stable floor. Mr. Covey seemed to think now that he had me and could do as he liked; but at that instant — where the spirit came from I cannot say — I made up my mind to fight, and acting on that resolve I seized Covey hard by the throat and rose up as I did so. He held on to me and I to him. My resistance was so completely unexpected that Covey seemed thrown off balance. He shook like a leaf. That gave me confidence, and I held him in a tight grip, drawing blood wherever my fingertips dug into him. Mr. Covey soon called out to Hughes for help. Hughes came, and while Covey held me he tried to tie my right hand. As he was at it, I watched my chance and gave him a hard kick just under the ribs. The kick truly sickened Hughes, so that he left me in Mr. Covey's hands. It not only weakened Hughes but Covey too. When Covey saw Hughes doubled over in pain, his nerve gave way. He asked if I meant to keep resisting. I told him I did, whatever came of it — that he had used me like a brute for six months, and I was determined to be used that way no longer. At that he tried to drag me toward a stick lying just outside the stable door, meaning to knock me down. But just as he leaned over to grab it, I caught him by the collar with both hands and snatched him suddenly to the ground. By this time Bill had come up. Covey called on him to help. Bill asked what he could do. Covey said, "Take hold of him, take hold of him!" Bill answered that his master had hired him out to work, not to help whip me, and so he left Covey and me to settle the fight ourselves. We went at it for nearly two hours. At last Covey let me go, puffing and blowing furiously, saying that if I had not resisted he would not have whipped me half so hard. The truth was, he had not whipped me at all. I reckoned he came out far the worse in the bargain, for he had drawn no blood from me, while I had drawn his. In all the six months I spent with Mr. Covey afterward, he never laid the weight of a finger on me in anger. Now and then he would say he had no wish to get hold of me again. "No," I thought, "you needn't — because you'll come off worse than you did before."

englishChanges.before: The holidays are part and parcel of the gross fraud, wrong, and cruelty of slavery. They are presented as a custom set up out of the slaveholders' kindness; but I say flatly that they spring from selfishness and are one of the crudest frauds worked upon the trampled slave. Masters do not grant the slaves this time because they would mind the loss of their labor during it, but because they know it would be dangerous to withhold it. You can see this in the fact that slaveholders like their slaves to spend those days in such a way that they are as glad to see them end as to see them begin. Their aim seems to be to sicken their slaves on the very idea of freedom by plunging them into the lowest forms of dissipation. For instance, slaveholders not only like to see a slave drink of his own accord, but will scheme in various ways to get him drunk. One scheme is to lay bets on their slaves over who can drink the most whisky without getting drunk, and in this way they get whole crowds to drink to excess. So when the slave asks for honest freedom, the cunning slaveholder, knowing how ignorant he is, cheats him with a dose of degrading dissipation, slyly labeled liberty. Most of us used to swallow it down, and the result was just what you would expect — many of us came to feel there was little to choose between liberty and slavery. We felt, and rightly enough, that we might almost as well be slaves to a man as to rum. So when the holidays were over, we staggered up out of the filth we had been wallowing in, took a deep breath, and marched off to the field — feeling, on the whole, rather glad to go, back from what our master had tricked us into mistaking for freedom into the arms of slavery again.

englishChanges.before: On January 1, 1834, I left Mr. Covey and went to live with Mr. William Freeland, who lived about three miles from St. Michael's. I soon found Mr. Freeland a very different man from Mr. Covey. He was not rich, but he was what would be called an educated southern gentleman. Mr. Covey, as I have shown, was a well-trained negro-breaker and slave-driver. Freeland, slaveholder though he was, seemed to have some regard for honor, some reverence for justice, and some respect for humanity. Covey seemed utterly dead to any such feelings. Mr. Freeland had many of the faults common to slaveholders — he was very hot-tempered and irritable — but in fairness I must say he was remarkably free of the degrading vices Mr. Covey was forever steeped in. Freeland was open and frank, and we always knew where to find him. Covey was a most cunning deceiver, who could be understood only by those sharp enough to see through his carefully laid frauds. Another advantage I gained in my new master was that he made no claim to religion, no profession of it — and that, in my view, was truly a great advantage. I say without the least hesitation that the religion of the south is nothing but a cloak for the most horrid crimes — a justifier of the most appalling barbarity, a sanctifier of the most hateful frauds, and a dark shelter under which the darkest, foulest, grossest, most hellish deeds of slaveholders find their firmest protection. If I were ever dragged back into the chains of slavery, then next to that enslavement itself I would count belonging to a religious master the worst calamity that could fall on me. For of all the slaveholders I have ever met, religious ones are the worst — the meanest and basest, the most cruel and cowardly of the lot. It was my wretched fate not only to belong to a religious slaveholder but to live in a whole community of such religionists. Right near Mr. Freeland lived the Rev. Daniel Weeden, and in the same neighborhood lived the Rev. Rigby Hopkins, both members and ministers in the Reformed Methodist Church. Among others, Mr. Weeden owned a woman slave whose name I have forgotten. For weeks at a time this woman's back was kept literally raw by the lash of that merciless, religious wretch. He used to hire hands. His rule was that whether a slave behaved well or behaved badly, it was a master's duty to whip him now and then to remind him of his master's authority. Such was his theory, and such was his practice.

englishChanges.before: I went straight home and told Master Hugh the story of how I had been wronged; and I am glad to say of him that, irreligious as he was, his conduct was heavenly compared with how his brother Thomas had behaved in a similar situation. He listened closely as I laid out the events that led up to the brutal attack, and he showed plainly how furious it made him. The heart of my once over-kind mistress melted into pity again. My swollen-shut eye and blood-covered face brought her to tears. She pulled up a chair beside me, washed the blood from my face, and, with a mother’s tenderness, bound up my head, laying a thin slice of fresh beef over the wounded eye. Seeing kindness once more from this, my once affectionate old mistress, was almost worth all my suffering. Master Hugh was greatly enraged. He let his feelings out by pouring curses on the heads of those who had done it. As soon as I had recovered a little from my bruises, he took me with him to Esquire Watson’s on Bond Street to see what could be done about it. Mr. Watson asked who had witnessed the assault. Master Hugh told him it had been done at midday in Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, where a large crowd of men were at work. “As to that,” he said, “the deed was done, and there was no question who did it.” Mr. Watson’s answer was that he could do nothing in the case unless some white man came forward to testify. He could issue no warrant on my word alone. Even if I had been killed in front of a thousand colored people, their combined testimony would not have been enough to arrest a single one of the murderers. Master Hugh, for once, was forced to admit that this state of things was too bad. Naturally, it proved impossible to find any white man willing to volunteer his testimony for me and against the white young men. Even those who may have felt for me were not prepared to do it. It took a kind of courage they did not have; for at just that time, the smallest show of humanity toward a colored person was branded as abolitionism, and that label exposed anyone who bore it to terrible dangers. The rallying cries of the bloody-minded in that region and in those days were, “Damn the abolitionists!” and “Damn the niggers!” Nothing was done, and probably nothing would have been done even if I had been killed. Such was, and such still is, the state of things in the Christian city of Baltimore.

Seeing kindness once more from this, my once affectionate old mistress, almost compensated for my suffering. Master Hugh was greatly enraged. He let his feelings out by pouring curses on the heads of those who had done it. As soon as I had recovered a little from my bruises, he took me with him to Esquire Watson’s on Bond Street to see what could be done about it. Mr. Watson asked who had witnessed the assault. Master Hugh told him it had been done at midday in Mr. Gardner’s ship-yard, where a large crowd of men were at work. “As to that,” he said, “the deed was done, and there was no question who did it.” Mr. Watson’s answer was that he could do nothing in the case unless some white man came forward to testify. He could issue no warrant on my word alone. Even if I had been killed in front of a thousand colored people, their combined testimony would not have been enough to arrest a single one of the murderers. Master Hugh, for once, was forced to admit that this state of things was too bad. Naturally, it proved impossible to find any white man willing to volunteer his testimony for me and against the white young men. Even those who may have felt for me were not prepared to do it. It took a kind of courage they did not have; for at just that time, the smallest show of humanity toward a colored person was branded as abolitionism, and that label exposed anyone who bore it to terrible dangers. The rallying cries of the bloody-minded in that region and in those days were, “Damn the abolitionists!” and “Damn the niggers!” Nothing was done, and probably nothing would have been done even if I had been killed. Such was, and such still is, the state of things in the Christian city of Baltimore.

englishChanges.before: I was quite disappointed by how things looked in general in New Bedford. The impression I had picked up about the character and condition of northern people turned out to be strangely mistaken. While I was a slave I had oddly imagined that few of the comforts, and almost none of the luxuries, of life were enjoyed in the north compared with what southern slaveholders enjoyed. I probably reached that conclusion from the fact that northern people owned no slaves. I assumed they stood about on a level with the non-slaveholding population of the south. I knew _those_ people were extremely poor, and I had grown used to thinking of their poverty as the inevitable result of their owning no slaves. Somehow I had absorbed the notion that without slaves there could be no wealth and very little refinement. So when I came north, I expected to find a rough, hard-handed, uncultivated population living in the most Spartan simplicity, knowing nothing of the ease, luxury, pomp, and grandeur of southern slaveholders. Given those guesses of mine, anyone who knows what New Bedford looks like can easily imagine how plainly I saw my mistake.

englishChanges.before: Now that I have read back over this Narrative, I notice that in several places I have spoken about religion in a tone that might lead readers who do not know my views to assume I oppose all religion. To head off that misunderstanding, I think it best to add this short explanation. Everything I have said against religion I mean to apply strictly to the slaveholding religion of this country, and not at all to Christianity itself; for between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ I see the widest possible difference—so wide that to accept the one as good, pure, and holy is necessarily to reject the other as bad, corrupt, and wicked. To be a friend of the one is to be an enemy of the other. I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ, and for that very reason I hate the corrupt, slaveholding, woman-whipping, cradle-robbing, partial, and hypocritical Christianity of this land. In fact, I can see no honest reason for calling the religion of this country Christianity at all. To me it is the worst of all misnamings, the boldest of all frauds, and the grossest of all slanders. There was never a plainer case of “stealing the livery of the court of heaven to serve the devil in.” I am filled with a loathing I cannot put into words when I look at the religious pomp and display around me, set against the horrible contradictions that go with it. Our ministers are men-stealers, our missionaries are woman-whippers, and our church members are cradle-robbers. The man who swings the blood-clotted cowskin all week stands in the pulpit on Sunday and calls himself a minister of the meek and lowly Jesus. The man who robs me of my wages at the end of every week meets me on Sunday morning as a class-leader, to show me the way of life and the path of salvation. The man who sells my sister into prostitution stands forth as the pious champion of purity. The man who calls it a religious duty to read the Bible denies me the right to learn to read the name of the God who made me. The man who is religion's great defender of marriage strips millions of its sacred protection and abandons them to wholesale corruption. The same man who praises the sacredness of the family bond is the one who scatters whole families—tearing apart husbands and wives, parents and children, sisters and brothers—and leaves the cabin empty and the hearth cold. We watch the thief preach against theft and the adulterer preach against adultery. Men are sold to build churches, women sold to support the gospel, and infants sold to buy Bibles for the Poor Heathen—all for the glory of God and the good of souls! The slave auctioneer's bell and the church-going bell ring in time with each other, and the bitter cries of the heartbroken slave are drowned out by the religious shouts of his pious master. Revivals of religion and booms in the slave-trade go forward hand in hand. The slave prison and the church stand close together. The clank of fetters and the rattle of chains in the prison, and the pious psalm and solemn prayer in the church, may be heard at the very same moment. The dealers in the bodies and souls of men set up their auction block in plain sight of the pulpit, and the two help each other along. The dealer hands over his blood-stained gold to support the pulpit, and the pulpit, in return, wraps his hellish trade in the clothing of Christianity. Here religion and robbery are allies—devils dressed in the robes of angels, and hell got up to look like paradise.

“Just God! and these are they,
Who minister at thine altar, God of right!
Men who their hands, with prayer and blessing, lay
On Israel’s ark of light.

“What! preach, and kidnap men?
Give thanks, and rob thy own afflicted poor?
Talk of thy glorious liberty, and then
Bolt hard the captive’s door?

“What! servants of thy own
Merciful Son, who came to seek and save
The homeless and the outcast, fettering down
The tasked and plundered slave!

“Pilate and Herod friends!
Chief priests and rulers, as of old, combine!
Just God and holy! is that church which lends
Strength to the spoiler thine?”

englishChanges.before: Dark and terrible as this picture is, I hold it to be strictly true of the overwhelming majority of professed Christians in America. They strain at a gnat and swallow a camel. Could anything describe our churches more exactly? They would be appalled at the idea of taking a sheep-stealer into fellowship, and yet they clasp a man-stealer to their communion, and brand me an infidel for finding fault with them over it. They attend to the outward forms of religion with Pharisaical strictness, while neglecting the weightier matters of the law—justice, mercy, and faith. They are always ready to make a sacrifice, but seldom to show mercy. They are the very people described as professing to love the God they have not seen while hating the brother they have seen. They love the heathen on the far side of the globe; they will pray for him, pay money to put a Bible in his hands and send missionaries to instruct him—while they despise and utterly neglect the heathen at their own door.

englishChanges.after:
“Come, saints and sinners, hear me tell
How pious priests whip Jack and Nell,
And women buy and children sell,
And preach all sinners down to hell,
And sing of heavenly union.

“They’ll bleat and baa, dona like goats,
Gorge down black sheep, and strain at motes,
Array their backs in fine black coats,
Then seize their negroes by their throats,
And choke, for heavenly union.

“They’ll church you if you sip a dram,
And damn you if you steal a lamb;
Yet rob old Tony, Doll, and Sam,
Of human rights, and bread and ham;
Kidnapper’s heavenly union.

“They’ll loudly talk of Christ’s reward,
And bind his image with a cord,
And scold, and swing the lash abhorred,
And sell their brother in the Lord
To handcuffed heavenly union.

“They’ll read and sing a sacred song,
And make a prayer both loud and long,
And teach the right and do the wrong,
Hailing the brother, sister throng,
With words of heavenly union.

“We wonder how such saints can sing,
Or praise the Lord upon the wing,
Who roar, and scold, and whip, and sting,
And to their slaves and mammon cling,
In guilty conscience union.

“They’ll raise tobacco, corn, and rye,
And drive, and thieve, and cheat, and lie,
And lay up treasures in the sky,
By making switch and cowskin fly,
In hope of heavenly union.

“They’ll crack old Tony on the skull,
And preach and roar like Bashan bull,
Or braying ass, of mischief full,
Then seize old Jacob by the wool,
And pull for heavenly union.

“A roaring, ranting, sleek man-thief,
Who lived on mutton, veal, and beef,
Yet never would afford relief
To needy, sable sons of grief,
Was big with heavenly union.

“‘Love not the world,’ the preacher said,
And winked his eye, and shook his head;
He seized on Tom, and Dick, and Ned,
Cut short their meat, and clothes, and bread,
Yet still loved heavenly union.

“Another preacher whining spoke
Of One whose heart for sinners broke:
He tied old Nanny to an oak,
And drew the blood at every stroke,
And prayed for heavenly union.

“Two others oped their iron jaws,
And waved their children-stealing paws;
There sat their children in gewgaws;
By stinting negroes’ backs and maws,
They kept up heavenly union.

“All good from Jack another takes,
And entertains their flirts and rakes,
Who dress as sleek as glossy snakes,
And cram their mouths with sweetened cakes;
And this goes down for union.”
